newsitem.title: FRANCE: U.N. secretary-general urges immediate Zaire aid.
newsitem.headline: U.N. secretary-general urges immediate Zaire aid.

text.p: U.N. Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali made a new appeal on Sunday for immediate world intervention to save starving refugees in Zaire, saying thousands were dying with every hour that passed.

"I make a new appeal to the members of the United Nations, to men and women of good will, to non-governmental organisations, to intervene today," Boutros-Ghali said during a stopover in Paris on his way to the World Food Summit in Rome.

"The international community must act immediately and every hour that passes leads to thousands of dead," he said of the disaster facing 1.2 million Hutu refugees with scant food or water after a Tutsi rebellion in eastern Zaire.
On Saturday, the U.N. Security Council called on U.N. members to lay the groundwork for a multinational force to help end the crisis in eastern Zaire but postponed a resolution setting up a force.
Boutros-Ghali, at Paris Charles de Gaulle airport, said this week's World Food Summit "takes on a special meaning when thousands of Africans are dying in the region of Kivu" in eastern Zaire.

France, which has led calls for a multinational force of between 4,000 and 5,000 troops to open relief lines to refugees in Zaire, linked any French participation to an agreement by a reluctant Washington to take part.

"An American presence in this operation seems absolutely essential," Foreign Minister Herve de Charette told France Info radio. "We will only do it with the participation of Europe, of Africa...and of the United States."

And de Charette, who accused the world last week of "spinelessness" in its reaction to the events in Zaire, spoke of the crisis in biblical proportions, saying: "There are the makings of the greatest tragedy in human history."
"The international community must assume its repsonsibilities," he added.
He denied France's drive in Zaire was tinged by lingering interests from France's colonial past in Africa. Zaire is a former Belgian colony in a French-speaking region of the continent.
"We have no interest in this affair other than the over-riding sense of the responsibility we must assume facing this human tragedy," he said.
Zairean President Mobutu Sese Seko, an ally of France, is currently convalescing on the French Riviera after surgery in Switzerland.

Rwanda's Tutsi-led government opposes any French role, since Paris sent 2,500 troops in 1994 on a mission to help end genocide. The Tutsis say the mission protected Hutus blamed for the slaughter and that many of them are now refugees in Zaire.

De Charette ruled out a repeat of the unilateral action of Operation Turquoise in 1994 in Rwanda, saying: "I believe it would not be possible, and it would also be counter-productive: it would have many negative effects."
